rv.q: A quietly devastating, gently funny and beautifully delivered piece of theatre, it shows us what it means to be one of those statistics.
In the end, this is that rare thing: a necessary play.
The play eloquently distils the galling outrage of a political situation in which, as a society, the most we choose to offer to a starving family is a soggy cheese sandwich.
Natasha Jenkins's set is a masterpiece of realism.
They radiate warmth, care and belief in people.
Alexander Zeldin remains an unparalleled chronicler of everyday pain and joy.
More often this is a heartbreaking portrayal of how the most vulnerable try to help one another.

Faith, Hope and Charity is essentially a play about disconnection, and something of a struggle in dramatic terms: structural linking is tenuous and moments of brewing conflict only go so far to create momentum.
This is a painful, profound portrait of people in despair that is worth investing in.

There’s no doubting that Faith, Hope & Charity is necessary theatre, its honesty unflinching, its compassion complete – rather that, for its message to travel as widely as it should, it doesn’t quite hold together.

The skilful naturalism of the show conceals the socioeconomic reality: a middle-class audience has hired a troupe of actors (who are also middle class) to pose as impoverished dropouts for a night of escapist amusement.
There are well-meaning contributions from the cast and creatives, but nothing can solve the short-comings of a verbose, static, lifeless script.

cn.t: Zeldin's quietly devastating trilogy closer about a struggling community centre divides critics. Most praise its naturalistic warmth and empathy for society's marginalized, though some find its bleak austerity portrait overly worthy.
